chapter.name: Exploring Mixtures and their Separation
chapter.blurb: Sweet crystals separating out of sugarcane juice and doctors testing a few drops of blood for malaria open a chapter on classifying mixtures as homogeneous or heterogeneous, and on expressing how concentrated a solution is using mass by mass, mass by volume and volume by volume percentage. It then works through the separation techniques each type of mixture calls for: crystallization, distillation (including fractional distillation) and paper chromatography for homogeneous mixtures, and a separating funnel, sublimation, centrifugation and coagulation for heterogeneous ones, before distinguishing solutions, suspensions and colloids by particle size, settling behaviour and the Tyndall effect that only the latter two show.

scope_in.item: Homogeneous mixtures (solutions): uniform composition throughout, e.g. sugar solution, vinegar (acetic acid in water), soda (carbon dioxide in water); heterogeneous mixtures: non-uniform, visibly distinct components, e.g. sand and water, oil and water

Gas mixtures are usually homogeneous because gas particles move freely and mix easily (e.g. hydrogen and oxygen); heterogeneous mixtures with a gas component include smoke, fog and dust in air; alloys as homogeneous mixtures of two or more metals, or a metal and a non-metal, formed by melting and mixing (e.g. brass ~80% copper/20% zinc, bronze ~80% copper/20% tin), not separable by physical methods
Solute, solvent and concentration (amount of solute dissolved in a given amount of solvent or solution)

Three percentage methods of expressing concentration and their formulas: mass by mass percentage (% m/m, used for solutions and some heterogeneous mixtures like milk powder or food labels), mass by volume percentage (% m/v, used for medicines like glucose solution or saline), volume by volume percentage (% v/v, used for miscible liquids like perfumes or vinegar), with worked examples

Solubility (maximum solute dissolving in a fixed solvent quantity at a given temperature) and saturated solution; solubility of solids generally increases with temperature, solubility of gases in liquids generally decreases with temperature; solubility curves (graph of solubility vs temperature)

Crystallization: cooling a saturated solution to deposit excess solute as crystals; used to separate two soluble solids (one in small quantity) and to purify solids, based on differences in solubility at different temperatures; Table 5.4 solubility data for potassium nitrate, sodium chloride, potassium chloride and ammonium chloride at various temperatures

Distillation: separates miscible liquids differing in boiling point by at least about 25 degrees Celsius by heating, vaporising and condensing (e.g. acetone 56 degrees Celsius and water 100 degrees Celsius); can also separate a liquid from dissolved solids; fractional distillation for boiling point differences less than 25 degrees Celsius, e.g. separating crude petroleum into petroleum gas, petrol, kerosene, diesel; Table 5.5 boiling points of water, acetone, alcohol, chloroform and benzene

Paper chromatography: separates mixture components using differences in how fast they move up wet chromatographic/filter paper carried by a solvent (usually water, sometimes another solvent like alcohol); used for inks, dyes and plant pigments

Immiscible liquids (e.g. mustard oil and water) settle into separate layers by density; separated using a separating funnel by draining the denser lower layer first, discarding the mixed middle portion, then collecting the upper layer

Sublimation: a solid (e.g. camphor, naphthalene, dry ice) changes directly to vapour on heating below its melting point, without passing through the liquid state; deposition is vapour changing directly back to solid on cooling; used to separate a sublimable solid from a non-sublimable one (e.g. camphor from sand)

Suspensions: heterogeneous, undissolved solid particles remain suspended, visible to the naked eye, particles larger than 1000 nm, settle on standing (e.g. sand in water, sawdust in water, tea leaves in water); when filtration is insufficient for cloudy/muddy water, centrifugation and/or coagulation are used

Centrifugation: spinning a mixture at high speed so centrifugal force moves heavier particles outward/downward while lighter liquid stays on top (e.g. separating plasma from blood cells); coagulation: adding a coagulant (e.g. alum to muddy water, acid to milk for paneer) to make fine particles clump together and settle, removed by decantation or filtration

Colloids: particle size between a solution and a suspension (1-1000 nm, vs less than 1 nm for a solution and more than 1000 nm for a suspension), particles stay uniformly dispersed and do not settle, dispersed phase and dispersion medium, examples milk, tomato sauce, ice cream, blood; emulsions (both phases liquid), e.g. milk/vanishing cream (oil-in-water), butter/cold cream (water-in-oil)
Tyndall effect: scattering of light by particles in a colloid or suspension, not shown by a true solution; first explained by John Tyndall

concepts.name: Classifying mixtures as homogeneous or heterogeneous
concepts.description: A mixture can be classified as homogeneous, with a uniform composition throughout like a solution, or heterogeneous, with visibly distinct, non-uniform components.
concepts.idea: A homogeneous mixture has the same composition throughout, while a heterogeneous mixture does not, and its separate components remain visible.
concepts.rule: You have learnt that a well-stirred mixture of sugar and water is equally sweet in the first sip and the last, because it has a uniform composition throughout; such a mixture is called a homogeneous mixture, or a solution. Vinegar (acetic acid in water) and soda (carbon dioxide in water) are other examples of homogeneous mixtures, and a solution always remains homogeneous. A stirred mixture of sand and water, by contrast, is not uniform: the sand particles are easily visible and settle with time, making it a heterogeneous mixture; oil and water, which form separate layers, are heterogeneous for the same reason. Gas particles are free to move in all directions, so they mix easily and uniformly, which is why most mixtures of gases, such as hydrogen and oxygen used as rocket fuel, are homogeneous; but smoke (solid particles in air), fog (liquid droplets in air) and dust in the air are heterogeneous mixtures with a gas as one component. Metals do not normally dissolve into one another at room temperature, but when melted at high temperature and mixed, they can form a homogeneous mixture called an alloy, which solidifies into a new material on cooling and cannot be separated by physical methods; brass (about 80% copper and 20% zinc) and bronze (about 80% copper and 20% tin) are common examples.
concepts.example: Sugar dissolved evenly in water is a homogeneous mixture, while sand stirred into water, which settles out and stays visible, is a heterogeneous mixture.

concepts.name: Concentration of a solution and how to express it
concepts.description: Concentration describes how much solute is dissolved in a solvent or solution, and can be expressed as mass by mass, mass by volume, or volume by volume percentage.
concepts.idea: The amount of solute dissolved in a fixed amount of solvent or solution is its concentration, expressed as a percentage in one of three ways depending on what is easiest to measure.
concepts.rule: In a solution, the substance that dissolves is the solute and the substance that dissolves it is the solvent; the amount of solute dissolved in a given amount of solvent or solution is its concentration. One common way to express concentration is as a percentage, in three forms. Mass by mass percentage (% m/m or % w/w) tells us how many grams of solute are present in 100 grams of the total solution, calculated as (mass of solute / mass of solution) x 100; it is used for homogeneous mixtures like a salt solution, and also for some heterogeneous mixtures such as milk powder or spice mixtures, and for labelling packaged foods. Mass by volume percentage (% m/v or % w/v) tells us how many grams of solute are present in 100 millilitres of solution, calculated as (mass of solute / volume of solution) x 100; it is used where measuring volume is easier than weighing, as with medicines like a 5% glucose solution or a 0.9% saline drip. Volume by volume percentage (% v/v) tells us how many millilitres of solute are present in 100 millilitres of solution, calculated as (volume of solute / volume of solution) x 100; it is used when two miscible liquids are mixed, as in perfumes, cosmetics, or vinegar (5% v/v acetic acid).
concepts.example: Dissolving 10 g of salt in 90 g of water gives 100 g of solution, so its mass by mass percentage is 10%.

concepts.name: Solubility, solubility curves and crystallization
concepts.description: Solubility is the maximum amount of solute that dissolves in a fixed amount of solvent at a given temperature, and crystallization uses how solubility changes with temperature to separate or purify solids.
concepts.idea: A saturated solution holds the maximum solute its solubility allows at that temperature, and cooling it lets any extra solute separate out as crystals.
concepts.rule: The maximum amount of solute that dissolves in a fixed quantity of solvent (100 g or 100 mL) at a given temperature is called its solubility at that temperature; a solution that cannot dissolve any more solute at that temperature is a saturated solution. Solubility depends on temperature: for a solid solute dissolving in a liquid solvent, solubility generally increases with temperature, while for a gas dissolved in a liquid, solubility generally decreases as temperature increases. A solubility curve, a graph of solubility against temperature, lets us read off and compare how different substances' solubility changes; for example, if a saturated solution of a compound at 60 degrees Celsius is cooled to 40 degrees Celsius, the solubility curve tells us how much less solute the solution can now hold, and the rest separates out as a pure solid, often as crystals with particles arranged in a regular geometric pattern. This process, called crystallization, can be used to separate two soluble solids when one is present in a much smaller quantity, and to purify solids, because it is based on differences in solubility of a substance at different temperatures.
concepts.example: Cooling a saturated solution of a compound from 60 degrees Celsius, where its solubility is 287 g per 100 g of water, to 40 degrees Celsius, where its solubility is only 241 g per 100 g of water, makes 46 g per 100 g of water separate out as crystals.

concepts.name: Distillation and paper chromatography
concepts.description: Distillation separates miscible liquids using differences in boiling point, and paper chromatography separates mixture components using differences in how fast they move on wet paper.
concepts.idea: Heating a mixture of miscible liquids until the lower-boiling one vaporises, then cooling the vapour back to liquid, separates them by their difference in boiling point.
concepts.rule: A homogeneous mixture of two miscible liquids can be separated by distillation: heating the mixture until the liquid with the lower boiling point vaporises, then cooling and condensing that vapour, which is collected as the distillate, while the other liquid, or a dissolved solid, remains behind. Distillation works when the two liquids' boiling points differ by at least about 25 degrees Celsius, as with acetone (about 56 degrees Celsius) and water (100 degrees Celsius). When the boiling point difference is less than 25 degrees Celsius, fractional distillation is used instead; this is how crude petroleum, extracted from the Earth's crust, is separated into fractions such as petroleum gas, petrol, kerosene and diesel at a refinery. Paper chromatography separates the components of a mixture using differences in how the components interact with the solvent and the paper: as a solvent, usually water, rises up a paper strip carrying an ink or pigment spot placed above the solvent level, the components separate into different coloured spots because they move at different speeds; if water does not work for a particular mixture, another solvent such as alcohol may be needed.
concepts.example: Because acetone boils at about 56 degrees Celsius and water at 100 degrees Celsius, a difference of 44 degrees Celsius, heating a mixture of the two lets the acetone vaporise and be condensed separately, well before the water boils.

questions.q: The process of separating two miscible liquids by heating until the lower-boiling liquid vaporises and then cooling the vapour back into a liquid is called ____.

because water always dissolves every pigment equally well

because the solid and liquid always have exactly the same boiling point

questions.a: The difference is 78 degrees Celsius - 61 degrees Celsius = 17 degrees Celsius, which is less than 25 degrees Celsius, so this mixture of alcohol and chloroform would need fractional distillation rather than simple distillation.

questions.q: Crude petroleum is a mixture of many liquids and gases with boiling points close to each other. Explain, using the ideas of distillation and fractional distillation, why fractional distillation rather than simple distillation is used to refine it into products like petroleum gas, petrol, kerosene and diesel.
questions.a: Simple distillation works well when the boiling points of the liquids in a mixture differ by at least about 25 degrees Celsius, but crude petroleum contains many components whose boiling points are close together, with differences of less than 25 degrees Celsius; fractional distillation is designed for exactly this case, separating components with small boiling point differences, which is why it is used at a petroleum refinery to obtain fractions like petroleum gas, petrol, kerosene and diesel from crude oil.
s: Simple distillation needs a difference of at least about 25 degrees Celsius
Crude petroleum's components have close boiling points

questions.q: Consider: (I) Distillation can be used to obtain a liquid from a solution containing dissolved solids. (II) Paper chromatography separates the components of a mixture mainly based on differences in their rate of movement carried by a solvent up the paper. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Both I and II

questions.q: Compare distillation and paper chromatography in terms of the kind of mixture each is normally used to separate.
questions.a: Distillation is normally used to separate miscible liquids, or a liquid from dissolved solids, based on differences in their boiling points, while paper chromatography is normally used to separate substances such as dyes, inks or plant pigments in a mixture based on differences in how fast they move when carried by a solvent up the paper.
s: Distillation - miscible liquids/boiling point
Chromatography - dyes/pigments/rate of movement

questions.q: A student has a mixture of two miscible liquids with boiling points 70 degrees Celsius and 74 degrees Celsius, and separately a mixture of black ink containing several dyes. Explain which separation technique from the chapter is suited to each mixture, and why neither technique would work well if swapped.
questions.a: For the two liquids with boiling points 70 degrees Celsius and 74 degrees Celsius, the difference is only 4 degrees Celsius, far less than 25 degrees Celsius, so fractional distillation, not simple distillation, is suited to separate them by their very close boiling points. For the black ink, paper chromatography is suited, since it separates the different coloured dyes based on how fast each moves up wet paper, not on boiling points. Distillation would not usefully separate the ink's dyes, since chromatography is not about boiling points at all, and paper chromatography would not work on the two liquids either, since it depends on a solid paper support carrying substances up it, not on separating liquids from each other by boiling.
s: Liquids - fractional distillation identified with reason
Ink - paper chromatography identified with reason
Explanation of why swapping would not work

questions.q: Do you think fractional distillation is always a 'better' method than simple distillation, or does it depend on the mixture being separated? Justify your answer.
questions.a: A reasoned answer is acceptable; for example, one might argue fractional distillation is not simply 'better' in general, since simple distillation is enough and easier to carry out when boiling points differ by more than 25 degrees Celsius, and fractional distillation is only needed for the harder case of components with close boiling points.
s: Position stated
Reason given

questions.q: Design a simple paper chromatography experiment, different from the chapter's ink activity, to find out how many coloured pigments are present in a green food colouring, describing the set-up and how you would read the result.
questions.a: Draw a pencil line about 2 cm from the bottom of a chromatographic or filter paper strip, place a small spot of the green food colouring at the centre of the line, and dip the lower end of the strip into a shallow layer of water, or alcohol if water does not work, in a jar, keeping the water level below the spot; as the solvent rises up the paper, it will carry the different coloured components of the green colouring at different speeds, and the number of separate coloured bands that appear on the paper tells you how many pigments are present in the mixture.
s: Set-up described - spot on line, dipped in solvent below the spot
Correct principle applied - components move at different speeds
How the result is read - number of separate bands equals number of pigments

concepts.name: Separating immiscible liquids and sublimation
concepts.description: A separating funnel uses density differences to separate two immiscible liquids, and sublimation uses a solid's direct change to vapour to separate it from a non-sublimable solid.
concepts.idea: Immiscible liquids settle into separate layers by density and can be drained apart using a separating funnel, while a sublimable solid can be separated from one that does not sublime by gentle heating.
concepts.rule: Some liquids, such as mustard oil and water, do not mix and are called immiscible liquids; when left undisturbed, they settle into two separate layers, with the less dense mustard oil forming the upper layer and the denser water forming the lower layer. A separating funnel is used to separate them: the stopcock is opened slowly to drain the denser lower layer (water) into a container, closed just before the water is fully drained to avoid collecting the mixed portion in between (which is discarded), and then opened again to collect the oil layer separately. Some solids, such as camphor, naphthalene, and solid carbon dioxide (dry ice), undergo sublimation: on heating, below their melting point, they change directly from the solid state to the vapour state without passing through the liquid state; on cooling, the vapour changes back directly into a solid without becoming a liquid, a process called deposition. Because a non-sublimable solid like sand does not sublime, heating a mixture of camphor and sand lets the camphor sublime away, leaving the sand behind, so sublimation is used to separate a sublimable solid from one that does not sublime.
concepts.example: Heating a mixture of camphor and sand makes white camphor deposits form on the inner wall of an inverted funnel, while the sand is left behind in the dish.

What remains after - sand and salt still mixed

questions.q: A student is given an unlabelled mixture and told it might be either (a) mustard oil and water, or (b) camphor and sand. Suggest one simple observation she could make to tell which type of mixture it is, and explain how each technique from the chapter would then apply to separate it.
questions.a: She could first observe whether the mixture is made of two liquids forming visible layers, or of solid particles mixed together. If it is two liquids in separate layers, it is likely mustard oil and water, an immiscible liquid mixture, which she would separate using a separating funnel by draining the denser water layer first and then collecting the oil. If it is a solid mixture, it is likely camphor and sand, which she would separate by gentle heating so the camphor sublimes into vapour, later collected as solid again by deposition, leaving the sand behind.
s: Observation described - liquid layers vs solid mixture
Correct method for oil-water - separating funnel
Correct method for camphor-sand - sublimation

questions.q: Do you think sublimation is a reliable way to fully purify camphor from sand in a single heating, or might some sand still end up mixed in? Justify your answer.
questions.a: A reasoned answer is acceptable; for example, one might argue it is generally reliable since only the camphor vapour rises and deposits on the funnel, leaving sand in the dish, though fine dust could in principle be carried up if heating is too vigorous, so care in heating gently matters.
s: Position stated
Reason given

questions.q: Design a simple set-up, using materials available at home, to demonstrate sublimation with naphthalene balls (mothballs) instead of camphor, describing your apparatus and how you would confirm sublimation occurred.
questions.a: Place a few crushed naphthalene balls in a small steel dish or bowl, cover it with an inverted funnel or a glass with its mouth plugged loosely with cotton to let a little vapour escape while collecting the rest, and heat the dish gently and briefly, with adult supervision, on a low flame or hot plate. Sublimation would be confirmed by seeing white solid deposits form on the inner, cooler surface of the funnel or glass, while no liquid puddle appears in the dish at any point.
s: Apparatus/set-up described
Heating step described, with safety noted
Confirmation described - solid deposit forms, no liquid stage

concepts.name: Suspensions, colloids and separating them: centrifugation, coagulation and the Tyndall effect
concepts.description: Suspensions, colloids and solutions differ mainly in particle size and settling behaviour, and techniques like centrifugation and coagulation separate the fine particles of a suspension or clear a cloudy mixture.
concepts.idea: Suspension particles are large, visible and settle over time; colloid particles are smaller, stay dispersed and scatter light (the Tyndall effect); centrifugation and coagulation are two ways to separate or clear such mixtures.
concepts.rule: In a suspension, such as sand stirred into water, the solid particles do not dissolve but remain suspended throughout the medium, are visible to the naked eye, and settle over time when left undisturbed; other examples include sawdust in water and tea leaves in water. When filtration alone cannot clear muddy water because some particles are too small, centrifugation and coagulation can help: centrifugation spins the mixture at high speed, and the resulting centrifugal force moves the heavier particles outward, where they settle at the bottom of the tube, while the lighter liquid stays on top, as used to separate plasma from blood cells; coagulation involves adding a coagulant, such as powdered alum to muddy water or an acid like lemon juice to milk to make paneer, which makes the fine suspended particles clump together so they settle by gravity and can then be removed by decantation or filtration. A colloid, such as milk, tomato sauce, ice cream, or blood, is neither a true solution nor a true suspension: its particles, 1 to 1000 nm, are larger than a solution's, less than 1 nm, but smaller than a suspension's, more than 1000 nm, and unlike a suspension's particles, a colloid's particles do not settle over time but stay uniformly dispersed as the dispersed phase within the dispersion medium; when both phases are liquids, the colloid is called an emulsion, such as milk (oil-in-water) or butter (water-in-oil). Both colloids and suspensions scatter a beam of light passing through them, a phenomenon called the Tyndall effect, first explained by the scientist John Tyndall, while a true solution does not show this effect.
concepts.example: A laser beam passed through a salt solution is invisible from the side, but the same beam is clearly visible passing through milk, because milk is a colloid that scatters light while a salt solution does not.

questions.q: A heterogeneous mixture in which solid particles remain undissolved but suspended throughout the medium, visible to the naked eye, is called a ____.
questions.a: suspension

questions.q: The scattering of light by particles in a colloid or a suspension is called the
questions.a: Tyndall effect

questions.q: The process of spinning a mixture at high speed so that heavier particles move outward and settle, while lighter liquid stays on top, is called
questions.a: centrifugation

questions.q: Which of these is NOT true about colloids, according to the chapter?

o: their particles settle down over time like in a suspension
their particle size is between 1 and 1000 nm
they scatter light, showing the Tyndall effect
milk and blood are examples of colloids

questions.a: because some particles are too small to be removed by filter paper or cloth
o: because some particles are too small to be removed by filter paper or cloth

because muddy water contains no suspended particles at all
because filtration works only on perfectly clear water

questions.q: A substance such as alum, which is added to muddy water to make fine particles clump together and settle, is called a ____.

questions.q: Milk, in which tiny droplets of fat are dispersed throughout a watery liquid, is an example of
questions.a: a colloid

questions.q: Why do colloidal particles, unlike suspension particles, not settle down over time?
questions.a: because colloidal particles are small enough to stay uniformly dispersed throughout the mixture
o: because colloidal particles are small enough to stay uniformly dispersed throughout the mixture
because colloidal particles are heavier than suspension particles
because colloids contain no particles at all
because colloidal particles dissolve completely like a true solution

questions.q: Explain why blood is classified as a colloid rather than a true solution or a true suspension.
questions.a: Blood's components can be separated by centrifugation like a suspension, but its particles, such as blood cells, are too small to be seen with the naked eye and do not settle on their own like a suspension's particles would; it is not a true solution either, since its particles are larger than a solution's and can scatter light; this in-between particle size and behaviour is what makes blood a colloid.
s: Not a true suspension - particles not visible/don't settle on their own
Not a true solution - particles larger, still scatter light

questions.q: A beam of light passed through a glass of clear sugar solution is not visible from the side, but the same beam is clearly visible passing through a glass of milk. This shows that
questions.a: milk is a colloid that scatters light, while the sugar solution is a true solution that does not
o: milk is a colloid that scatters light, while the sugar solution is a true solution that does not
milk is a true solution and the sugar solution is a colloid

questions.q: Powdered alum added to a beaker of muddy water causes the fine suspended particles to
questions.a: clump together (coagulate) and settle down
o: dissolve completely into a true solution
scatter light more strongly without settling

questions.q: A hospital needs to separate plasma from blood cells in a blood sample. Name the technique used and explain, in terms of particle movement, how it works.
questions.a: The technique used is centrifugation: the blood sample is spun at high speed, and the resulting centrifugal force causes the heavier blood cells to move outward and settle at the bottom of the tube, while the lighter plasma remains on top, allowing the two to be separated.
s: Technique named - centrifugation
Explanation - heavier particles move outward/settle, lighter liquid stays on top

questions.q: Paneer (cheese) is made from milk by adding lemon juice or vinegar. Explain this process using the term coagulation.
questions.a: The acid in the lemon juice or vinegar acts as a coagulant, causing the milk proteins to clump together (coagulate) and separate out as solid curds, which can then be strained from the remaining liquid to obtain paneer.
s: Acid acts as a coagulant on milk proteins
Proteins clump together and are separated out as paneer

questions.q: A student compares three mixtures: a salt solution, muddy water, and milk. Ranked from smallest to largest average particle size, the correct order is
questions.a: salt solution, milk, muddy water

questions.q: A water treatment plant receives cloudy river water. Using ideas from the chapter, describe a sequence of at least two techniques it could use to obtain clear water, and explain what each technique removes or does.
questions.a: First, a coagulant such as alum could be added to the cloudy water; this makes the very fine suspended particles clump together, coagulate, into larger clumps that settle down by sedimentation and can then be removed by decantation or filtration. After coagulation, the water could also be passed through filtration to remove any remaining larger particles and clumps, giving clearer water as a result; sewage treatment plants use a similar sequence of sedimentation, coagulation and filtration steps.
s: First technique named with what it does - coagulation, clumps fine particles
Second technique named with what it does - filtration/sedimentation, removes remaining particles
Overall sequence makes sense to produce clearer water

questions.q: Consider: (I) The particles in a suspension are larger than the particles in a colloid. (II) A colloid's particles settle down over time in the same way as a suspension's particles do. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only I

questions.q: Compare centrifugation and coagulation as two ways of dealing with a suspension of fine particles in water.
questions.a: Centrifugation separates fine particles from the liquid by spinning the mixture at high speed so the centrifugal force moves the heavier particles outward and down, without adding anything to the mixture, while coagulation works by adding a coagulant such as alum, which makes the fine particles clump together into larger clumps that then settle by gravity and can be removed by decantation or filtration.
s: Centrifugation - spinning, centrifugal force, no substance added
Coagulation - coagulant added, particles clump and settle

questions.q: Explain, using particle size and behaviour on standing, why the chapter distinguishes solutions, colloids and suspensions as three separate categories rather than treating them all simply as 'mixtures of two substances'.
questions.a: The three categories differ mainly in particle size and in what happens to the particles over time: a solution has particles smaller than about 1 nm that stay dissolved and never settle or scatter light; a colloid has particles between about 1 and 1000 nm that stay uniformly dispersed without settling but do scatter light, showing the Tyndall effect; a suspension has particles larger than about 1000 nm, visible to the naked eye, that settle down over time when left undisturbed. Because these differences affect how each type behaves, and which separation technique will work on it, treating them as three distinct categories rather than one broad group of mixtures is scientifically useful.
s: Solution described - very small particles, no settling, no scattering
Colloid described - intermediate size, no settling, but scatters light
Suspension described - large particles, visible, settles

questions.q: Do you think the Tyndall effect alone is enough to tell a colloid apart from a suspension, or would you need another test as well? Justify your answer.
questions.a: A reasoned answer is acceptable; for example, one might argue the Tyndall effect alone is not enough, since both colloids and suspensions scatter light, so an additional test, such as leaving the mixture undisturbed to see whether the particles settle over time as in a suspension or stay dispersed as in a colloid, is also needed to tell them apart.
s: Position stated
Reason given

questions.q: Design a simple home demonstration, different from the alum-and-muddy-water activity in the chapter, that would show a friend the difference between how a suspension and a colloid behave when left undisturbed for a day.
questions.a: Prepare two containers: one with a spoonful of fine sand stirred into water, a suspension, and one with a spoonful of milk stirred into water, a colloid. Leave both undisturbed for a day without touching them, then observe: the sand-water mixture should show sand settled clearly at the bottom with clearer water above it, while the milk-water mixture should still look uniformly cloudy throughout with no separate layer, showing that suspension particles settle over time while colloidal particles remain evenly dispersed.
s: Two mixtures set up - a suspension and a colloid example
Left undisturbed and observed after a set time
Correct expected difference described - settling vs staying dispersed
